power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Specifying Innateness in Infant Development: A Framework for Theory-Building Based on Co-Determination

text.text: Infant research has often treated early neural and behavioral expression as a privileged window into the initial state of the mind, with early-emerging capacities sometimes uncritically taken as broad evidence of innate knowledge.

This paper evaluates the strength of such inferences through four intersecting lenses: genetics and epigenetics, cultural evolution, definitional precision, and historical and contemporary standards of scientific explanation and falsifiability.

It distinguishes among several non-equivalent forms of innateness, including claims about representational content, architectural or processing biases, developmental canalization, and maturational timing.

In place of broad or underspecified appeals to innateness, it advances greater specificity in accounts of co-determination as a framework for theorybuilding that encourages delineation of biological constraints, experiential inputs, cultural ecologies, developmental timing, and interactive mechanisms proposed to produce a given outcome, as well as patterns of variation that would support or challenge those claims.
The central aim is to provide a more tractable and testable basis for theorizing about the initial state of the infant mind.

Infant research has long treated early behavior as a privileged window into the initial state of the mind, inviting strong claims that capacities observed in the first months of life reflect innate representational knowledge (e.g., Bloom, 2010; Carey, 2009; Chomsky, 1980; Spelke, 2000; Spelke & Kinzler, 2007; Spelke, 2024a Spelke, , 2024b)).

text.text: Highly impactful programs in core knowledge, language acquisition, conceptual development, natural pedagogy, numeracy, and morality have often taken early emerging behavioral patterns as evidence for pre-specified knowledge structures that scaffold later learning and development (e.g., Bloom, 2010; Carey, 2009; Feigenson et al., 2004; Gergely & Csibra, 2013; Gleitman, 2020; Spelke & Kinzler, 2007).

text.text: At the same time, developmental science has cultivated influential alternatives, including work on ontogenetic niches (West & King, 1987), experiential canalization (Gottlieb, 1991), probabilistic epigenesis (Gottlieb, 2004), connectionism (Elman et al., 1996), and extended brain-body-behavior networks (Byrge et al., 2014).

text.text: It is likely that most infant theorists would agree that both biologically grounded constraints and developmental experience contribute to the emergence of knowledge.

The aim of this paper is therefore neither to defend nor to reject innateness as an explanatory principle, but instead to examine whether innatist claims are sufficiently integrated with evidence on gene-culture interaction, cultural evolution, contextually limited sampling, and standards of definitional precision and falsifiability.
On this basis, the paper argues for a more explicit approach to theory-building grounded in clearly specified principles of co-determination.
Innatist accounts of development are varied, diverse, and non-equivalent.

For example, a claim that infants possess innately specified conceptual content that is manifest early in development is not equivalent to a claim that learning is shaped by biologically grounded biases in attention and perception.
Nor are these claims identical to the notion that a developmental outcome is canalized across a range of environments, or that it emerges according to a relatively robust maturational timetable.
In addition, evidence that challenges one level of innateness does not necessarily challenge others.

For example, evidence of prenatal speech learning may qualify any inference that newborn language preferences reflect experience-independent representational content, but it does not, by itself, rule out biologically prepared auditory biases, experience-expectant tuning mechanisms, or innate architectural constraints that shape language learning.

The argument developed here is directed primarily at strong representational nativism and at under-specified innatist mechanisms in more moderate accounts (for an example, see Bai et al., 2025, discussed below), rather than at the broader claim that biological constraints and biases contribute to developmental change.

text.text: Strong claims about core knowledge, innate morality, and related early emerging capacities, attributing rich innate structure to infants, have had outsized influence on how infant findings are used to theorize about the origins of human cognition.
Their influence has been tremendously generative for the field.

However, they have also encouraged a recurring inferential pattern in which infant behavioral expression is treated as evidence for a richly endowed initial state without an equally detailed account of developmental mechanisms, sufficient connection with socioecological diversity, engagement with interactive developmental conditions, and perhaps most critically, without a precise articulation of the specific conditions under which the claim could be falsified.
Innateness itself is variously defined as a concept (see Table 1 for a summary).

text.text: As Mameli and Bateson (2011) argue, "innateness" has been synonymized with genetic specification, evolutionary shaping, the absence of learning, developmental robustness, and modularity, definitions that are often treated interchangeably or, at the very least, seldom explicitly distinguished.

text.text: Consistent with the goal of this paper to encourage a more explicit elaboration of how innate contributions to development are defined and to clarify the kinds of evidence required to adequately test those claims, the paper draws on genetics and epigenetics, cultural evolution, sampling diversity, and theories of scientific determinism.
The aim is not simply to replace a broad claim of innateness with a similarly broad claim of codetermination.

Rather, the article argues for more precisely specified and measurable approaches to codetermination as a source of insight into developmental mechanism in the form of theories and/or models that identify which biological biases, input structures, developmental timetables, and feedback processes impact development; how they interact; and under what conditions particular outcomes are projected to vary or remain stable.
This is not the first attempt to question the basis for strong innatist accounts of development.

Empiricist, constructivist, neuroconstructivist, connectionist, dynamic-systems, and developmental robotics approaches have repeatedly challenged strong innateness interpretations by showing how domain-relevant structure can emerge from interactions among bias, input, embodiment, task demands, and developmental timing.

This work spans language, object cognition, social cognition, theory of mind, causal reasoning, and categorization, and has shown that apparently early or abstract competencies can sometimes be generated by domain-general learning mechanisms operating over structured input (Benton, 2025; Berthiaume et al., 2013; Christiansen & Curtin, 2005; Cohen et al., 2002; Elman, 1993; Mareschal et al., 1999; McClelland & Thompson, 2007; Morton & Munakata, 2002; Munakata et al., 1997; Rakison & Lupyan, 2008; Schlesinger & Casey, 2003; Van Overwalle, 2010; Westermann et al., 2007).

text.text: Rather than denying that infants possess rich early representations of objects, number, geometry, and social agents, this account relocates many of those representations from conceptual reasoning (or more broadly, nonperceptual processes) to perception.

On this view, infant findings traditionally interpreted as evidence of precocious conceptual reasoning may instead reflect perceptual processes that are fast, automatic, and sensitive to particular features of sensory input.
This proposal poses an important challenge to the inference that sophisticated infant behavior necessarily reflects conceptual knowledge.

At the same time, it illustrates a central theoretical distinction relevant to the present discussion: recharacterizing a capacity as perceptual rather than conceptual does not resolve questions about its developmental origins or innateness.
Indeed, the core-perception account appears to retain, or at least does not explicitly reject, that these capacities emerge early, are species-typical and universal, and are rooted in human biology.
Thus, while the account challenges claims about the nature and source of infants' knowledge, it leaves questions about innateness largely unresolved.

Like much of the literature Bai et al. (2025) seek to reinterpret, the account is principally concerned with the nature of internal processes rather than with the range of developmental ecologies in which those processes emerge.
text.formatted: Like much of the literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bai et al. (2025)</ref> seek to reinterpret, the account is principally concerned with the nature of internal processes rather than with the range of developmental ecologies in which those processes emerge.

text.text: It therefore leaves largely unaddressed how variation in prenatal environments, early experience, gene-culture interactions, cultural practices, and historically narrow sampling might shape or constrain the development of these perceptual systems, or what evidence would distinguish species-typical perceptual organization from perceptual organization that is canalized through common developmental environments.

A co-determination framework would instead ask which components of these perceptual systems are biologically constrained, how they are calibrated through prenatal and postnatal experience, how they vary across developmental contexts, and what empirical evidence would distinguish pre-specified perceptual organization from rapidly constructed perceptual organization.

Thus, the empirical challenge in characterizing innateness is not simply to ask whether a behavior appears early or consistently in infants, but to specify the conditions and dynamics that would be sufficient-or insufficient-to produce it.

An important charge for the field is to articulate scientific frameworks that specify how co-determination can be articulated with specificity and precision, and how hypothesis emerging from these frameworks can be subjected to robust empirical scrutiny.
In the following section, the interactive roles of genetics, epigenetics, and culture are discussed as joint factors that would inform such a framework.

text.text: Developmental processes thus may reflect gene-culture co-development responsive to this variation rather than experience-independent representational specification.
Culture shapes the environments in which genes act from the earliest moments of life.

This does not begin at birth: culture organizes pregnancy through norms around work, nutrition, stress exposure, social support, medical care, household structure, and shared expectations about caregiving.
These patterned conditions shape the prenatal environment within which gene expression and fetal development unfold.
Maternal stress during pregnancy and its impact on the developing infant provides a clear illustration of this.

Crucially, prenatal stress is culturally patterned through work conditions, social support, discrimination, nutrition, access to care, household structure, and locally shared expectations about pregnancy and caregiving (Buffa et al., 2018; Coussons-Read, 2013).

(2018) note that much of the existing evidence has come from high-income countries, even though low-and middle-income countries often face greater maternal and infant health burdens, including higher rates of low birthweight and prematurity.

(2018)</ref> note that much of the existing evidence has come from high-income countries, even though low-and middle-income countries often face greater maternal and infant health burdens, including higher rates of low birthweight and prematurity.

text.text: Across studies from 24 countries, prenatal stress was assessed through measures such as perceived stress, stressful life events, anxiety, depression, common mental disorders, occupational stress, trauma, and cortisol, and was examined in relation to gestational age, preterm birth, birthweight, smallfor-gestational-age status, temperament, motor development, behavior, physical growth, and child health.

The conclusions of this study underscore that prenatal stress is frequently embedded in local cultural ecologies of health care access, poverty, nutrition, gendered labor, social support, political instability, and exposure to violence or disaster, making it an especially clear example of how structural conditions, intertwined with geography and culture, can permeate developmental pathways before birth.

These broader structural conditions are also evident within high-income countries, where racialized stress and unequal access to protective resources have been implicated in persistent disparities in birth outcomes, including higher rates of low birth weight, infant mortality, and small-for-gestationalage births among African American women compared with White women (Coussons-Read, 2013).
text.formatted: These broader structural conditions are also evident within high-income countries, where racialized stress and unequal access to protective resources have been implicated in persistent disparities in birth outcomes, including higher rates of low birth weight, infant mortality, and small-for-gestationalage births among African American women compared with White women <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Coussons-Read, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, although some prenatal risk factors, such as smoking and hypertension, predict low birth weight across racial groups, stress exposure and low social support appear to have especially pronounced associations with adverse birth outcomes among African-American women, suggesting that sociocultural factors associated with minority status can intensify the developmental consequences of prenatal stress.
The developmental significance of these disparities lies in the fact that contextual exposure can become biologically embedded before birth.
In terms of mechanisms, elevated maternal cortisol and stress-related hormones cross the placenta and alter the fetal environment, influencing infant stress regulation and neurodevelopment.

For example, newborns whose mothers experienced depression and anxiety during pregnancy showed increased DNA methylation of the NR3C1 glucocorticoid receptor promoter in newborn cord blood; this methylation pattern predicted heightened cortisol reactivity in infancy, suggesting that prenatal stress had already shaped infant stress responsivity before birth (Oberlander et al., 2008).

text.text: Similarly, there is converging evidence that prenatal maternal distress is associated with altered expression and epigenetic regulation of genes related to stress-response pathways, which in turn predict differences in infant temperament, affect regulation, and later risk for internalizing problems (Monk et al., 2012).

text.text: These findings provide a mechanism for how cultural and structural conditions can become biologically embedded before birth.
The same patterned ecologies often continue after birth, creating continuity between prenatal exposure and the early postnatal environments in which regulation, attention, and learning unfold.

Epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, histone modification, and alterations in chromatin accessibility, provide a biological pathway through which early caregiving, stress, nutrition, and sensory environments shape neural and behavioral development.

For example, Meaney and colleagues' rodent studies demonstrated that variation in maternal licking and grooming led to stable methylation changes at the glucocorticoid receptor (NR3C1) promoter, producing long-term differences in stress reactivity (Meaney, 2010; see also Weaver et al., 2004).

text.text: Parallel findings in humans show that infants exposed to parental stress and anxiety during pregnancy are associated with altered methylation patterns in stress-regulatory genes in the placenta, and that these methylation patterns are in turn associated with newborn neurobehavior, including stress regulation, muscle tone, and lethargy (Conradt et al., 2013).

text.text: These findings are directly relevant to culture because prenatal stress and caregiving consistency are not randomly distributed across individuals; they are shaped by culturally organized expectations, social support systems, family structures, economic insecurity, racialized stress, migration histories, and institutional access to care (Coussons-Read, 2013; Dunkel Schetter & Tanner, 2012;  National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2020).

text.text: Thus, environments beginning in utero do not simply activate innate programs; instead, they configure the molecular landscape within which development unfolds.
Human "natural experiments" also suggest that environmental influences on development begin well before birth.

One of the most studied cases is the Dutch Hunger Winter, a famine that occurred in the Netherlands during the winter of 1944-1945, when pregnant women experienced severe caloric restriction during different windows of gestation.

Six decades later, individuals exposed to the famine around the time of conception showed lower DNA methylation of the imprinted IGF2 gene than their unexposed same-sex siblings, whereas those exposed only late in gestation did not (e.g., Heijmans et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Six decades later, individuals exposed to the famine around the time of conception showed lower DNA methylation of the imprinted IGF2 gene than their unexposed same-sex siblings, whereas those exposed only late in gestation did not (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Heijmans et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Early prenatal famine exposure has also been linked to later health outcomes such as coronary heart disease and schizophrenia, although clear causal pathways have yet to be established.
Nonetheless, the Dutch Hunger Winter illustrates that what might later be treated as innate individual differences may partly reflect prenatal environmental exposure.
Taken together, these findings have four key implications for innateness.
First, infants are never truly "acultural": prior to birth they are already embedded in patterned developmental niches.
Second, genes do not act apart from cultural variation, but in continuous interaction with it.
Third, epigenetic mechanisms provide biological pathways through which early experience shapes later behavior.
Fourth, early appearance or cross-population recurrence do not by themselves establish experience-independence.
Species-typical outcomes can emerge from species-typical niches just as readily as from pre-specified representational content (Gottlieb, 1991; West & King, 1987).
text.formatted: Species-typical outcomes can emerge from species-typical niches just as readily as from pre-specified representational content <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Gottlieb, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">West & King, 1987)</ref>.

text.text: Because gene-culture interactions operate not only within development but also within and across generations within a cultural context, their implications for innateness extend directly into the domain of cultural evolution.
Cultural inheritance can offer a wider and faster route to adaptation than genetic inheritance because ideas, norms, and practices can spread and change far more quickly than genes.
Whereas genetic change in humans is tied to the long interval between generations, cultural change might happen within moments, across years, or over lifetimes.

In many animal species, and especially in humans, localized rituals, learned traditions and social practices shape how individuals behave, survive, and reproduce, making culture a potent evolutionary influence.

Over long periods, these culturally driven behaviors appear to have fed back onto human biology, contributing to shifts (e.g. in speech anatomy, the mental capacities that support learning from others, and internalized social norms) (Waring & Wood, 2021).
text.formatted: Over long periods, these culturally driven behaviors appear to have fed back onto human biology, contributing to shifts (e.g. in speech anatomy, the mental capacities that support learning from others, and internalized social norms) <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Waring & Wood, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The expansion and increasing complexity of human societies, alongside our rise as a dominant species, suggest that cultural inheritance is a major driver of evolutionary change on a global scale.

Some have argued that culture acts as a second inheritance system that co-evolves with genetic evolution, producing traits that emerge from long histories of gene-culture co-adaptation rather than from purely genetic mechanisms (Muthukrishna et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Some have argued that culture acts as a second inheritance system that co-evolves with genetic evolution, producing traits that emerge from long histories of gene-culture co-adaptation rather than from purely genetic mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Muthukrishna et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This means that behaviors observed in infants today reflect developmental outcomes shaped by evolved cultural practices that have exerted selection pressures over generations.
Thus, what might look like an innate behavior could instead be products of cultural evolution, both independent from and interdependent with genetic transmission.
A further complication arises from the covariance of genes and culture.
Parents transmit both genes and culturally patterned practices to their children, making it difficult to assign developmental outcomes cleanly to one source or the other (Scarr & McCartney, 1983).
text.formatted: Parents transmit both genes and culturally patterned practices to their children, making it difficult to assign developmental outcomes cleanly to one source or the other <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Scarr & McCartney, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: Because these influences are inherently entangled, developmental pathways cannot be neatly partitioned into biological and cultural origins.
This has important consequences for how perceived universality (i.e. sameness across respondents) is interpreted as evidence of innateness.
Universality is a descriptive claim about the recurrence of a pattern across groups, whereas innateness is an arguably stronger explanatory claim about why that pattern emerges.
Even genuinely widespread outcomes may reflect recurring developmental environments and similar cultural affordances rather than biological pre-specification.
Moreover, universality itself may be mis-inferred when the evidentiary base is narrow.

Patterns observed repeatedly in relatively homogeneous samples can appear species-general simply because relevant cultural, linguistic, socioeconomic, and ecological variation has not been sampled (Singh et al., 2023; Singh & Rajendra, 2024).
text.formatted: Patterns observed repeatedly in relatively homogeneous samples can appear species-general simply because relevant cultural, linguistic, socioeconomic, and ecological variation has not been sampled <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Singh et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Singh & Rajendra, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: As these survey studies demonstrate, many infant studies do not report basic information about participants' ancestry, community of descent, socioeconomic circumstances, or even the site of testing, making it difficult to establish the true breadth of the evidence.
Studies that do report such information reveal a pronounced and enduring concentration of White participants from a limited range of Euro-American contexts.

Claims of universality-and the use of apparent universality as evidence for particular innateness claims-are therefore often advanced on the basis of evidence drawn from a restricted and often incompletely characterized set of populations.
A behavior may appear widespread or species-typical within these contexts because humans within like contexts can inherit and inhabit a common set of cultural and ecological affordances.
This does not mean that behavior is prespecified or invariant.
The field's history of relying on narrow and underspecified samples therefore limits universalist interpretations of infant behavior that often motivate innatist theory.
The problem is compounded when the populations under study share similar histories of cumulative cultural evolution.

Standardized schooling, similar family structures, shared institutions, and other culturally evolved practices can produce developmental environments that are more alike than they initially appear (Uchiyama et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Standardized schooling, similar family structures, shared institutions, and other culturally evolved practices can produce developmental environments that are more alike than they initially appear <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Uchiyama et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, variation in culturally relevant experiences may be compressed in the literature, making behaviors appear more universal within the sampled populations than they would across the broader range of human developmental contexts and populations.
The Scarr-Rowe effect offers a concrete illustration of this: in some U.S. samples, the heritability of general intelligence is substantially higher among high-SES than low-SES families.
Samples from Europe and Australia show far more uniform heritability of general intelligence scores across SES strata (D. C. Rowe et al., 1999; Scarr-Salapatek, 1971; Tucker-Drob & Bates, 2016).

text.text: This pattern implies that what looks like a genetic contribution to intelligence may be in part contingent on the structure of socioeconomic inequality within the broader environment.

Applied to infant research, this means that when researchers draw on similarly situated samples to make claims about human cognitive architecture, they are often generalizing from a relatively small region of the much wider backdrop of human developmental environments.

Without sampling a wider range of gene-culture configurations, it is difficult to know whether an observed pattern reflects a species-typical developmental process or one that depends on recurrent environmental conditions.
These empirical challenges also expose a conceptual challenge.

Because genes, culture, and development are so deeply intertwined, the evidence reviewed above does not simply complicate empirical tests of innateness; it also complicates what researchers mean when they invoke the term.

Whether observations are taken to support or challenge innateness depends in part on whether innateness is taken to mean representational content, developmental robustness, architectural constraints, maturational timing, or some other property.
Greater semantic precision is therefore a prerequisite for interpreting empirical findings and for evaluating competing developmental explanations.

A major complication of invoking innateness is that it is irregularly defined. Griffiths (2002) points out that scientists and philosophers use innateness to convey a range of meanings: present at birth, not learned, genetically specified, developmentally canalized, species-typical, environmentally invariant, amongst others. Mameli and Bateson (2006) similarly offer many candidate definitions of innateness; from this, they conclude that none gives a satisfactory, unified scientific notion, and that researchers often use them interchangeably, implying conceptual equivalence across different definitions (see Table 1).

text.text: One way forward is to disaggregate at least five separable claims that are often aggregated: (1) innate content is present early; (2) architectural or processing biases constrain learning; (3) privileged learning biases or preparedness make some inputs easier to acquire than others; (4) developmental outcomes are canalized across a range of environments; and (5) maturation follows a relatively robust timetable.
These are distinct and non-substitutable conceptual claims, and evidence that challenges one does not automatically challenge the others (Elman et al., 1996; Mameli & Bateson, 2011).
text.formatted: These are distinct and non-substitutable conceptual claims, and evidence that challenges one does not automatically challenge the others <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Elman et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Mameli & Bateson, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: As noted, the empirical base for many innateness claims is narrow, further complicating any of these claims.
But the problems of limited diversity compounds when innateness is not clearly defined.
Much infant work implicitly equates availability at birth with innateness.
Availability at birth means only that a capacity can be observed in newborns under the conditions they have experienced.
On one hand, this does not, by itself, establish that the capacity emerged independently of experience.
On the other hand, evidence of learning, including prenatal learning, should not be treated as a blanket refutation of innateness claims.
Many theoretical frameworks allow that biologically prepared systems require input to be expressed, tuned, or calibrated; in this sense, learning and innateness are not mutually exclusive.
Prenatal sensitivity to speech, for example, is not evidence against the possibility of innate languagerelevant structure per se.
Rather, it challenges the narrower inference that language-related preferences observed at birth are entirely experience-independent.

In such cases, it is critical to clearly articulate whether the available input was informative for the capacity in question, and what prior biases, architectures, or constraints would still be needed to explain the observed behavior.

For example, auditory, visual, social, and motor capacities differ in the kinds of input available before and immediately after birth and thus differ in the kinds of developmental explanations that are plausible.
This point is important for cases such as early visual preferences.

Some early visual preferences may ultimately be best explained by low-level perceptual biases, orienting mechanisms, maturational constraints, or rapid postnatal tuning; others may prove to require stronger biological constraints.
Face preferences in newborns provide an important example of why early emergence should not be equated with fully innate representational content.

Newborns show reported attentional biases toward faces and face-like configurations, including preferences for upright face-like stimuli, open eyes, direct gaze, attractive faces, and the mother's face.
However, these findings do not by themselves establish that newborns possess an innate representation of faces.

As Slater et al. (2010) note, some accounts interpret newborn face preferences as arising from general properties of the immature visual system, including sensitivity to stimuli with more elements in the upper visual field, top-heavy structure, or congruent arrangements of visual elements.
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Slater et al. (2010)</ref> note, some accounts interpret newborn face preferences as arising from general properties of the immature visual system, including sensitivity to stimuli with more elements in the upper visual field, top-heavy structure, or congruent arrangements of visual elements.

text.text: On this view, what appears to be a preference for "faces" may initially reflect sensitivity to visual configurations that overlap with faces along a range of dimensions, rather than a pre-specified representation of faces as a social category.

Indeed a recent systematic review and metaanalysis found only limited and inconsistent support for a face preference in newborns tested before postnatal face exposure, with most evidence coming from newborns whose preferences may already reflect this experience (Wilkinson et al., 2026).

text.text: A developmental-systems interpretation further obscures the inferential leap from newborn preference to innate capacity. Reynolds and Roth (2018) argue that early attentional biases for faces are best understood as emerging from interactions among organismic constraints, stimulus properties, prenatal and postnatal sensory experience, arousal, and the developing attention system.
text.formatted: A developmental-systems interpretation further obscures the inferential leap from newborn preference to innate capacity. <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Reynolds and Roth (2018)</ref> argue that early attentional biases for faces are best understood as emerging from interactions among organismic constraints, stimulus properties, prenatal and postnatal sensory experience, arousal, and the developing attention system.

text.text: Newborns are not experience-free organisms: they arrive with prenatal auditory experience, including familiarity with the mother's voice and native-language rhythm, and this prior experience may shape postnatal visual attention in multimodal social contexts.
Similarly, findings that only a few hours of postnatal interaction can support preference for the mother's face indicate that early face preferences may be calibrated by experience.

Relatedly, Scott and Arcaro (2023) propose a domain-relevant developmental framework in which face specialization emerges through experience operating over general neurobiological mechanisms, providing a mechanistic account of how domain-selective organization can develop without requiring fully pre-specified face representations.
text.formatted: Relatedly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Scott and Arcaro (2023)</ref> propose a domain-relevant developmental framework in which face specialization emerges through experience operating over general neurobiological mechanisms, providing a mechanistic account of how domain-selective organization can develop without requiring fully pre-specified face representations.

text.text: The developmental trajectory of face processing also argues against treating newborn preferences as definitive evidence for a fully specified innate face system. Slater et al. (2010) describe the newborn "face space" as broadly rather than narrowly tuned.

(2010)</ref> describe the newborn "face space" as broadly rather than narrowly tuned.

text.text: Newborns around the world do not yet show the same race-, gender-, or species-specific tuning that emerges over the first year of life.
With repeated exposure, infants develop preferences for familiar classes of faces and become more accurate at recognizing ownrace and own-species faces.

However, three months after birth, infants raised in multiracial contexts demonstrate an early other-race preference (Singh et al. 2022) whereas those raised in monoracial contexts demonstrate an early own-race preference (Kelly et al. 2005).
text.formatted: However, three months after birth, infants raised in multiracial contexts demonstrate an early other-race preference <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Singh et al. 2022)</ref> whereas those raised in monoracial contexts demonstrate an early own-race preference <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Kelly et al. 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Within these contexts, infants with personalized multiracial interaction demonstrate a more pronounced other-race preference with age.

These varied findings are consistent with experiential canalization: early biases may direct attention toward socially relevant input, but that input then may shape the systems that processes visual information including faces.
This distinction is relevant to innateness claims more generally.

If a newborn preference can be explained by low-level perceptual salience, prenatal sensory integration, rapid postnatal learning, or broad attentional biases that become specialized through experience, then the stronger and more useful claim must specify what is proposed to be innate, how it operates mechanistically, how experience modifies it, and what evidence would falsify the proposed mechanism.

The central claim of this paper is therefore not that developmental science should replace all biological explanation with learning, but that theories should specify the level of explanation at issue and relevant sources of input for the particular domain and target behaviors under study.
These examples also reflect that immediately after birth, infants are embedded in active social and cultural environments that vary significantly along multiple axes.

This view is consistent with developmental-systems accounts that characterize infant learning as both embodied and embedded, emerging through recurrent feedback among infant action, caregiver response, and structured environmental contexts (Tamis-LeMonda & Masek, 2023).
text.formatted: This view is consistent with developmental-systems accounts that characterize infant learning as both embodied and embedded, emerging through recurrent feedback among infant action, caregiver response, and structured environmental contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Tamis-LeMonda & Masek, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Such variation supplies the very input through which perception, attention, and social expectations are calibrated in the earliest weeks and months.
Together, these considerations underscore that even the earliest observable capacities are already the products of structured developmental histories.
Despite the challenges outlined above, innateness remains an appealing explanatory framework for infant researchers.

This appeal may partly reflect the field's intellectual history: much of infant research developed around innatist questions and theoretical frameworks when methodological tools and experimental paradigms were less sophisticated, infants' capacities for learning were less well understood, and the implications of restricted sampling for developmental explanation were less widely acknowledged.
Although tools, paradigms, and knowledge have become increasingly sophisticated, the refinement of innateness as an explanatory principle has not always developed in step with these advances.
The field often continues to cast the infant as an instrument with which to examine psychological organization independent of experience.

For example, Geraci et al. (2025) argue that evidence from human newborns, who have "extremely limited experience with sociomoral phenomena" relative to older infants, suggests that selective responses to aspects of the social world may emerge independently of experience.

(2025)</ref> argue that evidence from human newborns, who have "extremely limited experience with sociomoral phenomena" relative to older infants, suggests that selective responses to aspects of the social world may emerge independently of experience.

text.text: Similarly, Geraci et al. (2026) refer to newborn visual sensitivities as an innate capacity to detect communicative intent.

text.text: Other recent work has made related appeals to newborn or very early sensitivities as bearing on innate empathy, multimodal understanding, or number knowledge (Davidov et al., 2025; Lorenzi et al., 2025; Streri & de Hevia, 2023).

text.text: Core knowledge remains an active contemporary theory rather than a historical position.
It continues to be developed in contemporary work (e.g., Spelke, 2024a Spelke, , 2024b) ) and is placed in focus in theoretical challenges, including those raised by Bai et al. (2025).

text.text: The mere fact that core knowledge theory remains both actively advanced and contested underscores its continuing influence in current developmental science.
In these traditions, infants are presumed valuable precisely because they are presumptively closer to the biological starting point than older children and adults.
Many foundational theories and experiments in the field are therefore implicitly or explicitly organized around these particular accounts of innateness.
These traditions also interact with methodological limitations.

In the absence of detailed, mechanistic models of how fetal learning, early perceptual biases, caregiver input, and cultural practices could jointly generate early abilities, it becomes easy to default to the idea that the structure must already be present in some form.

Against the messy reality of gene-culture co-development, innatist narratives may seem tractable, not because alternative accounts are impossible in principle, but because current developmental models are often too underspecified to compete with them.
This is reinforced by a deeply ingrained cultural image of the infant as an unconditioned or "pure" organism, pre-social, pre-cultural, and largely unimpacted by learning.

Even though there is now strong evidence for fetal learning and for dense social and cultural input from birth onward, much theorizing still leans on the intuition that very young infants have not yet had enough experience for cultural explanations to be plausible.

That intuition is reinforced by a broader rationalist tradition in philosophy and cognitive science in which early competence is treated as evidence for inborn structure, as well as by behavioral-genetic findings showing substantial heritability for some psychological traits.

For example, Plomin and von Stumm's (2018) review of the genetics of intelligence argues that individual differences in intelligence are substantially heritable and increasingly predictable from genome-wide polygenic scores.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Plomin and von Stumm's (2018)</ref> review of the genetics of intelligence argues that individual differences in intelligence are substantially heritable and increasingly predictable from genome-wide polygenic scores.

text.text: Such findings are important, but they are often taken to carry more developmental significance than heritability estimates can support.

Heritability estimates describe sources of variation within particular populations and environments; they often do not specify the developmental mechanisms through which traits emerge, nor do they establish that particular abilities are innate, experience-independent, or unmalleable across environmental and cultural contexts.
Taken together, these forces make innateness an attractive explanatory position.

It is built into the foundational theories, fills explanatory gaps where detailed developmental accounts are lacking, resonates with traditional images of infants as culturally unconditioned, and appears to harmonize with some approaches to heritability.

This history underscores the value of more explicitly specifying what is claimed to be innate, the developmental mechanisms proposed to produce it, and the evidence that would distinguish competing accounts.
There is no doubt that most if not all aspects of infant development must reflect biological constraint, and some version of an innateness-based account is necessary.
Specific concerns arise, however, when claims are made of a "representational infant" with complex conceptual systems that are posited to exist prior to, and largely independent of, experience.
Those stronger claims are often inferred from experimental effects rather than from mechanistic accounts of how such structures could arise through development.
A more productive approach may be to ask what, exactly, is being claimed about observed competencies.
It then becomes easier to evaluate what evidence would support it, what evidence would challenge it, and what sort of developmental model would be required.
In this way, claims about innateness evoke classic debates about falsifiability.
Scientific claims must expose themselves to the risk of refutation: they should rule out possible observations that would show them to be wrong (Popper, 1959).
text.formatted: Scientific claims must expose themselves to the risk of refutation: they should rule out possible observations that would show them to be wrong <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Popper, 1959)</ref>.

text.text: Claims should not be so broadly framed that an unbounded set of outcomes can be retroactively reinterpreted as consistent with the claim, leaving no conceivable pattern of data that could disconfirm it.
In infant research, some innateness claims are framed so broadly that almost any developmental outcome can be reinterpreted as "expression" of an innate structure.
Kuhn's subsequent analysis provides insight into the impact of falsifiability: whether claims are treated as falsifiable in practice depends on their role within a paradigm (Kuhn, 1962).
text.formatted: Kuhn's subsequent analysis provides insight into the impact of falsifiability: whether claims are treated as falsifiable in practice depends on their role within a paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Kuhn, 1962)</ref>.

text.text: Within any given dominant research tradition, causal accounts (e.g., appeals to innateness) can function as a partial explanation; variation in findings (e.g., null findings in infants; non-replication) may be absorbed by appealing to methodological variation or adding auxiliary explanations, rather than prompting rejection of the dominant framework.
In their strongest and least specified forms, some claims about innateness in the infant literature fall short on both counts.

By Popper's account, many claims of innateness may not satisfy basic definitions of hypotheses at all, because they are framed so broadly that no realistic pattern of developmental data could falsify them.
They instead function as default explanations, justified by the presumption that infants are socially and culturally unconditioned, rather than by having survived serious attempts at refutation.

In Kuhnian terms, innateness often functions less as a testable hypothesis and more as part of the protected core of a long-accepted paradigm, insulated from challenges by its historical entrenchment and the inertia of existing theory-building practices.

By contrast, a more disciplined innateness hypothesis might try to specify what is supposedly built-in, when it should be observable, and what developmental factors would fail to surface the expression of innate capacities.

Innateness is not automatically unfalsifiable, but it becomes scientifically interesting when embedded in theories that generate clear and potentially disconfirmable predictions about development, variation, and plasticity, rather than operating as an explanation that derives from a range of equivalently possible interpretations of data.
Moving beyond the limitations of innateness claims does not mean relinquishing the guiding questions that have advanced infant research over decades.

It means creating clearer definitions of innateness, aligning inferences about innateness with methods and findings, and considering putative innate structure within a broader multiplex of factors that co-determine development.
In the present usage, codetermination does not simply mean "everything matters," nor is it intended to function as a formal theory on its own.

It refers to a framework in which outcomes are explained by specifying interacting classes of factors: (a) organismic constraints, predispositions, and architectures; (b) the form, timing, and distribution of input available to the infant; (c) caregiving and cultural ecologies; (d) gene-culture dynamics; (e) the mechanisms through which these factors interact to produce change; and (f) the kinds of variation expected within and across ecologies.

This distinction between a framework and a theory is important: frameworks can organize attention toward relevant concepts, processes, timescales, and methods, but their scientific value depends on how explicitly they are translated into testable theoretical claims (Stallworthy et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This distinction between a framework and a theory is important: frameworks can organize attention toward relevant concepts, processes, timescales, and methods, but their scientific value depends on how explicitly they are translated into testable theoretical claims <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Stallworthy et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The same explanatory standard should apply to co-determination.
Evidence that experience influences development is no more sufficient as an explanation than evidence that a behavior appears early is sufficient to establish innateness.

A well-specified co-determination account must therefore identify experience that is informationally relevant to the target behavior, specify the mechanism through which that experience acts together with organismic constraints, generate predictions about developmental or contextual variation, and identify evidence that would count against the proposed account.
In this sense, co-determination is not a complete theory in itself, but a constraining framework for constructing and comparing developmental theories on common empirical ground.

The requirement for symmetrical explanatory standards can be illustrated by recent evidence that newborns preferentially attend to prosocial over antisocial interactions. Geraci et al. (2025), for example, reported that newborns looked longer at prosocial than antisocial events, including helping relative to hindering.
text.formatted: The requirement for symmetrical explanatory standards can be illustrated by recent evidence that newborns preferentially attend to prosocial over antisocial interactions. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Geraci et al. (2025)</ref>, for example, reported that newborns looked longer at prosocial than antisocial events, including helping relative to hindering.

text.text: This presents a demanding test for a co-determination account because demonstrating that newborns have extensive prenatal developmental histories, relevant to this particular outcome, is not sufficient to explain this particular response (but see Lourenco, 2026, for alternative explanations).
text.formatted: This presents a demanding test for a co-determination account because demonstrating that newborns have extensive prenatal developmental histories, relevant to this particular outcome, is not sufficient to explain this particular response (but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Lourenco, 2026</ref>, for alternative explanations).

text.text: Prenatal stress, maternal physiology, auditory learning, or epigenetic modification do not themselves provide information about helping and hindering, and the visual relations instantiated in these displays are unavailable prenatally.

A co-determination account would therefore have to identify developmentally available information relevant to the distinction, such as structure in newborns' early postnatal experience of agents, goals, contingent action, or approach and withdrawal and specify how learning operating over that input, together with any proposed perceptual or attentional biases, could generate differential responding to the displays.
It should further predict how the response would vary with relevant experience or ecology and identify evidence that would falsify this explanation.

If the preference proved robust despite meaningful variation in relevant postnatal experience, and models constrained by infants' approximated input could not generate the effect without additional built-in structure, then knowable and documented evidence of experience would be insufficient to explain the phenomenon.

Such a finding would strengthen the case for biologically prepared constraints, while leaving open the further question of what those constraints consist of, for example, representational content, attentional or perceptual biases, learning preparedness, or architectural organization.
The point is therefore not to privilege experiential explanation, but to require competing developmental accounts to meet the same standards of specificity and falsification.
A second and related future direction concerns the empirical base of the field.
A stronger basis for claims about the origins of human cognition and innate structure requires data from infants in a wide range of cultural, linguistic, socioeconomic, and ecological contexts.
Agreement across multiple crosscultural settings is not, by itself, confirmation of universality or innateness.

A concerning response to calls for greater sampling diversity has been the tendency to test relatively small samples of infants in one high-resource and one low-resource setting, often using tasks developed and implemented by researchers from the high-resource context, and to infer universality from similar patterns of responding across the two groups.
Thus, diversification is not simply a matter of adding research sites.

Thoughtful diversification includes building infrastructures for global developmental research, supporting cross-site collaborations, partnering with researchers and communities in underrepresented settings from conception onward, and adopting transparent standards for reporting sociodemographic and cultural information.
In this respect, enterprises such as ManyBabies have immense value as we wrestle with sampling diversity (Frank et al., 2017).
text.formatted: In this respect, enterprises such as ManyBabies have immense value as we wrestle with sampling diversity <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Frank et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: It also includes harmonizing measures across laboratories while preserving contextual relevance, reporting cultural and ecological variables in theoretically meaningful ways, and creating incentive structures that reward collaborative, interdisciplinary, and community-engaged work.

A lack of diversity in infant samples means that what appears to be innate and thus universal features of development may instead reflect the boundaries of the widely studied populations, settings, and methods used to map the infant mind rather than boundaries of the infant mind itself (Singh, 2026).
text.formatted: A lack of diversity in infant samples means that what appears to be innate and thus universal features of development may instead reflect the boundaries of the widely studied populations, settings, and methods used to map the infant mind rather than boundaries of the infant mind itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Singh, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Diversification is thus a necessary condition for claims of universality and of innateness.
Third, the assumption that newborns are effectively experience-free is difficult to sustain.
By extension, newborns cannot be treated as uniquely privileged "test beds" for innateness simply because they have had little postnatal experience.
Birth is not the beginning of development, and the presence of a behavior at birth does not, on its own, establish that the behavior emerged independently of experience.
As discussed, newborns arrive with developmental histories, and in at least some domains, those histories are already consequential.
Clear evidence comes from perceptual and sensory development and its later expression.

In the auditory domain, fetuses hear filtered versions of maternal speech, learn about the rhythm and prosody of the ambient language, and show postnatal preferences for the mother's voice, familiar speech passages, and language rhythms to which they were exposed prenatally (DeCasper & Fifer, 1980; DeCasper & Spence, 1986; Mehler et al., 1988; Partanen et al., 2013).
text.formatted: In the auditory domain, fetuses hear filtered versions of maternal speech, learn about the rhythm and prosody of the ambient language, and show postnatal preferences for the mother's voice, familiar speech passages, and language rhythms to which they were exposed prenatally <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(DeCasper & Fifer, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">DeCasper & Spence, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Mehler et al., 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Partanen et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Related evidence comes from chemosensory learning.

Flavors from the maternal diet can be transmitted through amniotic fluid, and prenatal exposure can shape infants' later acceptance of those flavors; newborns also show attraction to odors associated with amniotic fluid, suggesting that olfactory experience before birth can guide early orientation and feeding-related behavior (Mennella et al., 2001; Varendi et al., 1996).
text.formatted: Flavors from the maternal diet can be transmitted through amniotic fluid, and prenatal exposure can shape infants' later acceptance of those flavors; newborns also show attraction to odors associated with amniotic fluid, suggesting that olfactory experience before birth can guide early orientation and feeding-related behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Mennella et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Varendi et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: These examples make clear that early-emerging preferences should not be treated as evidence of experience-independent structure simply because they are present at birth.
As noted above, they also should not prohibit innateness claims.

Prenatal exposure to speech, for example, bears directly on claims about newborn language preferences, voice recognition, rhythm, and prosody because auditory and linguistic information is available before birth.

By contrast, the same evidence does not by itself explain early-emerging visual, object-based, or social sensitivities, for which the relevant sources of input may be absent, degraded, or available only after birth.

Those capacities require their own domain-specific analyses of what input was available, whether that input contained the structure needed to support the observed behavior, and what prior biases, architectures, or maturational constraints would still need to be posited.

Thus, the argument is not that early experience broadly refutes innateness, but that claims about innate structure should be evaluated against the specific input histories, learning opportunities, and mechanistic demands of the target domain.

Fourth, a co-determination perspective also encourages resisting the partitioning of infant development into seemingly independent constructs such as genetics, language exposure, caregiving, or culture.
Instead, it favors models that treat these as interacting sources of constraint and change.

For instance, when infants classified as bilingual or monolingual are compared on developmental outcomes, a host of intertwined factors-migration histories, socioeconomic conditions, caregiving practices, community networks, and educational resources-shape both groups in ways that make it impossible to interpret differences as the product of language exposure alone.
In other words, the measured variable is often one element of a wider constellation of ecological and child-internal influences.

This approach parallels calls in language development to integrate accounts of learning mechanisms with the nested social and cultural contexts in which language input is encountered (M. L. Rowe & Weisleder, 2020).
text.formatted: This approach parallels calls in language development to integrate accounts of learning mechanisms with the nested social and cultural contexts in which language input is encountered (M. L. <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Rowe & Weisleder, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A co-determination model should therefore specify which of these factors are treated as relevant to the mechanism of interest, how they are expected to interact, and where the model predicts convergence versus divergence across contexts.
Fifth, human infants develop in culturally organized niches that have themselves been shaped by long histories of cultural evolution.
Virtually every aspect of infants' experience is part of the developmental process, not merely a backdrop against which genes independently do their work.
Accordingly, most single-laboratory infant experiments support local, situated interpretations and do not straightforwardly license innatist or universal claims.
It then becomes natural to ask how the cultural environments within which infants learn are themselves intertwined with underlying patterns of genetic variation.
The idea that cultural and genetic variation can become tightly intertwined over time has gained increasing traction in human population research.
For example, when cultural communities maintain stable, distinctive practices, these cultural boundaries can shape social networks and patterns of assortative mating.
Over generations, such processes can lead to fine-scale genetic structure variation that is aligned with cultural and linguistic boundaries, even within a single country and a single language.

A recent study by Pichkar and Creanza (2023) illustrates this dynamic by showing that English dialect boundaries co-localize with fine-grained genetic clusters across the UK, suggesting that dialect communities have historically constrained who interacts with whom and who has children with whom.
text.formatted: A recent study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Pichkar and Creanza (2023)</ref> illustrates this dynamic by showing that English dialect boundaries co-localize with fine-grained genetic clusters across the UK, suggesting that dialect communities have historically constrained who interacts with whom and who has children with whom.

text.text: Extrapolating this to infant learners, this implies that early language learners in different regions are likely to inherit both region-specific linguistic input and genetic ancestry associated with language use in these regions.

The extent to which such region-based genetic variation shapes infant language learning processes or outcomes remains an open empirical question and will require designs that can query interactions of cultural experience and genetic variation.
Seen in this light, evaluating innateness is an ambitious proposition that is not the province of any single researcher, laboratory, method, or domain area.
It is unrealistic to expect that a single lab, working with a narrow range of paradigms in a limited set of populations, could establish innateness or universality on its own.
The average infant scientist simply does not have access to the breadth of samples, methodological diversity, or analytical toolkit needed to do so.
These considerations point toward a more consilient and collaborative science of infancy that explicitly integrates evidence across disciplines.

The most informative accounts of infant development will likely be those that link genetic predispositions, learning processes, and the structure of cultural input within a single probabilistic framework, drawing on insights from the psychological sciences, cultural evolution, developmental biology, behavioral epigenetics, cognitive anthropology, sociology, and related disciplines.

This integrated framework should also attend to developmental timing: experience may have different effects depending on whether it occurs during prenatal development, early postnatal calibration, sensitive periods, or later periods of increasing specialization (Nelson & Gabard-Durnam, 2020).
text.formatted: This integrated framework should also attend to developmental timing: experience may have different effects depending on whether it occurs during prenatal development, early postnatal calibration, sensitive periods, or later periods of increasing specialization <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Nelson & Gabard-Durnam, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Although the field may not yet be fully equipped-conceptually, methodologically, or infrastructurally-to evaluate such complex multi-level models, particularly given its current tendency toward "solo science," greater cross-disciplinary integration provides a useful direction for future work.

Finally, alongside these conceptual and empirical shifts, we advocate a stronger normative commitment to parsimony in theorizing and in parallel, for greater intellectual humility in communicating claims.

When confronted with striking early abilities, it is tantalizing to posit rich interpretation (a practice, implicitly encouraged by many high-impact outlets); a more conservative strategy is to first ask whether a simpler account, grounded in known perceptual biases, fetal and postnatal experience, and task demands, could plausibly produce the observed behavior.

Work on scientific writing shows that seemingly small stylistic choices can lead readers to treat findings as broader and more general than the underlying, often narrow, samples warrant (DeJesus et al., 2019).

text.text: In parallel, metascientific work on intellectual humility argues that credible science depends on foregrounding uncertainty and limitations, and on resisting incentive structures that reward overconfidence in exposition (Hoekstra & Vazire, 2021).

text.text: For claims about innateness, this suggests that modest, tightly constrained, data-derived interpretations should be treated as a strength rather than a weakness, and that stronger claims about universality or inborn structure should be explicitly marked as long-term hypotheses that often require convergent evidence across methods, models, and populations.

We are now seeing rapid advances in machine learning, developmental robotics, and computational modeling that shed unprecedented light on the origins of learning in both artificial and biological systems (Cangelosi & Schlesinger, 2015; Orhan & Lake, 2024; Oudeyer & Smith, 2016).
text.formatted: We are now seeing rapid advances in machine learning, developmental robotics, and computational modeling that shed unprecedented light on the origins of learning in both artificial and biological systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cangelosi & Schlesinger, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Orhan & Lake, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Oudeyer & Smith, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Combined with finegrained behavioral and neural data, these approaches give us tools for tracing how induction, memory systems, embodiment, and regularities in the input can generate surprisingly sophisticated behavior over time, sometimes mimicking human behaviors often described as innate.
We can now query within an input-dependent learner how knowledge arises, how learning stabilizes, and what kinds of priors are actually required for generalization.

Contemporary machine learning also offers a way to make innateness claims about infant learning more precise by decomposing them into assumptions about inductive bias, input dependency, and learnability.
This logic has clear precedents in earlier connectionist and developmental modeling traditions (Elman et al., 1996).
text.formatted: This logic has clear precedents in earlier connectionist and developmental modeling traditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Elman et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: In computational terms, "innate structure" corresponds to architectural and prior constraints, while the environment is instantiated as distributions of visual, linguistic, or social input.
Learning is implemented through optimization over that input (Lake et al., 2017; Stojnić et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Learning is implemented through optimization over that input <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Lake et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Stojnić et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Models trained on this logic have produced mixed but informative results.
Some show that fairly generic architectures can learn useful visual representations from naturalistic, child-directed input (Orhan & Lake, 2024).
text.formatted: Some show that fairly generic architectures can learn useful visual representations from naturalistic, child-directed input <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Orhan & Lake, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Others suggest that some built-in structure may still be needed: a model of intuitive physics, for example, learned key physical expectations only when it represented the world in terms of objects (Piloto et al., 2022) and current models still fall short of infants on tests of commonsense psychology (Stojnić et al., 2023; for a review of computational approaches to theory of mind, see Langley et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Others suggest that some built-in structure may still be needed: a model of intuitive physics, for example, learned key physical expectations only when it represented the world in terms of objects <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Piloto et al., 2022)</ref> and current models still fall short of infants on tests of commonsense psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Stojnić et al., 2023</ref>; for a review of computational approaches to theory of mind, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Langley et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These models cannot tell us directly what infants' brains represent or how they work; however, they can help clarify which constraints must be built in, which regularities can be learned from structured input, and offer some predictions that would distinguish among competing innateness claims.

Taken together, the evidence reviewed in this paper suggests that innateness, in its broad and underspecified form, is not a sufficiently robust explanatory principle for understanding infant development.

This conclusion is directed most strongly at claims that infer rich representational content from early behavior while leaving the developmental route to that behavior largely unspecified and to more moderate accounts that invoke innateness without clear specification of mechanisms.
Earlyemerging patterns arise from developmental processes in which culturally organized experiences can already have begun to shape development in interaction with biological mechanisms.

Philosophical analyses of falsifiability further suggest that many strong innateness claims remain insulated from refutation when they are framed too broadly or when the relevant level of explanation is left ambiguous.
A developmental science that seeks to explain the origins of infant capacities should therefore adopt a more explicit framework of co-determination.

Such a framework treats infants' abilities as emerging from dynamic, historically situated interactions among biological biases, prenatal and early postnatal experience, caregiving ecologies, cultural practices, and longer-run gene-culture dynamics.
It also encourages closer integration with research on cultural evolution, behavioral genetics, epigenetics, developmental theory, and computational modeling.
Advancing expository practices such as parsimony in interpretation, specificity in writing, and humility in inference-making is likely to benefit the future of the field as well.

None of this represents a retreat from the central questions that animated innateness debates; instead, it is a proposal for addressing them with defined concepts, robust developmental models, and more disciplined modes of inference.

practical test of an innateness claim could therefore require at least four specifications.
First, the claim should identify the level of innateness being proposed, such as representational content, architectural bias, learning preparedness, canalization, or maturational timing.
Second, it should specify the relevant input structure, including what prenatal, postnatal, cultural, and relevant information was available to the infant.

Third, it should state what pattern of developmental variation would be expected across infants with different input structures or ecological contexts and test for these patterns using situated methods, analytic techniques, and inferences.
Fourth, it should identify what evidence would count against the proposed innate mechanism.
Without the final specification, innateness is not a testable developmental hypothesis.
